O Most kind JESUS, my love, my salvation, and my consolation. O most faithful lover of mankind <note>original: "amator hominum"; a title reflecting Christ’s deep affection for humanity.</note>, my creator and my redeemer: light of my heart, solace of my spirit, and medicine of my soul; how much I owe you, my God! How highly you have valued me, my creator—you who formed me from nothing in your image and likeness: you who purchased me at such an inestimable price, redeemed me with such great labor, and, enduring me with patience for so many years, spared me even as I persisted in my iniquities. With so many benefits, you have drawn me to yourself and followed after me with such great kindness; and by your divine grace, on countless occasions...

with all my strength I open my heart to you. Grant, I beseech you, that it may be pierced by the rays of your divine love <note>original: "charitatis"; in this context, it refers to *caritas*, the highest form of Christian love directed toward God and neighbor.</note>, and be illuminated by the splendors of your divine brightness, so that I may more deeply perceive the very depths of my soul, and see and acknowledge how far I am from you, my God. May I also see which faults and which vices hinder me from your love and service, and make me unworthy to receive the inflow of your divine grace into my soul. To such an extent, O Lord my God, have you embraced and surrounded me with your immense gifts, benefits, and graces <term>graces: the original "charifmatibus" refers to spiritual gifts or talents granted by God for the benefit of the community.</term>, and especially by your incomprehensible love, that I am unable to hide myself from the heat of your love, or to restrain my spirit from your praise.

Indeed, my heart longs to praise you and to give thanks to you with every faculty I possess; my spirit exults greatly in your praise, and my soul magnifies you <note>A reference to the "Magnificat," the song of the Virgin Mary in Luke 1:46-55, a cornerstone of daily prayer.</note>, because your grace is great upon me. But who am I, O most high and almighty creator, that I should dare to praise you? How indeed shall I dare to open my most impure mouth, defiled by so many vices, to proclaim your power and strength? Nay, what can I even think of you—you who are immense, invisible, incomprehensible, and inscrutable—in...

the angelic spirits wonderfully rejoice and take delight in the contemplation of you: such great strength, that you make the earth tremble with a single look: such admirable power <note>original: "virtus"; in this context, it refers to divine power or efficacy rather than just moral virtue.</note>, that you produced heaven and earth by a word, and all creatures <term>creaturae: in theological writing, this refers to any created thing—human, animal, or inanimate—rather than just "monsters" or "animals."</term> are subject to your will: such great richness, that whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven and earth belongs to you directly, and you rule and govern everything contained in them without care or anxiety: finally, such great goodness and mercy above all, that your mercy <note>original: "misericordia"</note> is over all your works. When, therefore, the Lord JESUS had instructed His beloved disciples in true humility through both His words and His example, and the time of His <term>Passion<gloss>From the Latin "passio," referring to the period of Christ's intense suffering and crucifixion.</gloss></term> was now approaching, He wished to teach them—and all of us—His other virtue. ### A Devout Exercise on the Passion of the Lord.

#### CHAPTER VI.

When the time was now drawing near for the Lord **JESUS** to pass from this world to the Father, a <term>Testament<gloss>original: "Testamento"; referring both to a "Last Will and Testament" and the "New Testament" established through the Eucharist</gloss></term> had already been established by him, as if by a most faithful father with his beloved disciples. He had left to them the chief and most excellent good that his fatherly heart could devise: namely, his most sacred body as food and his precious blood as drink. (He certainly did this so that he might provide them a sure sign of his most burning love, and leave behind him an eternal memorial or monument of his passion, death, and all his works; and finally, that he might hand over an extraordinary, certain, and indeed precious <term>pledge of his future glory<note>original: "futurę glorię suæ pignus"; a phrase traditionally used in the Church to describe the Eucharist as a foretaste of Heaven</note></term>.)

He was often accustomed to gather there with those same disciples for the sake of prayer. And he said to them: "Sit here, watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation." <meta>The text begins mid-word, completing "prepared".</meta>...red his heart, so that he might forget his own **human fragility**. However, temptation overturned all of this, so that he who had boastfully raised himself above himself might now humbly cast himself down below himself and hold himself in contempt. Now, left to himself, he might learn what he was unable to recognize while he was in that state of spiritual fervor. Indeed, he had offered himself to God and was allowing God to work within him; but that sublime structure which God desired to build in him could not be raised up unless the **fragile ground** was first uncovered, and then a deep and humble foundation was set in place. 

For as soon as he was looked upon by Christ <note>A reference to Luke 22:61: "The Lord turned and looked at Peter."</note> and perceived the light of His **grace** in the <term>depth of his soul<gloss>Latin: *fundus*. In mystical theology, the "depth" or "ground" of the soul is the innermost essence where the human spirit meets the Divine.</gloss></term>, he followed that light. He yielded to the touch and inspiration of the Spirit, doing what he was being prompted to do—namely, turning himself away from created things and turning toward the light he felt within himself. Through this light, he was led to <term>self-knowledge<gloss>Latin: *cognitio sui*. ### CHAPTER XVII.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut decorative initial 'D' featuring floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

AFTER THIS, Annas sent Jesus bound to Caiaphas, who was the high priest <term>pontifex summus: the supreme religious leader in Jerusalem</term> of that year. At his house, the chief priests, scribes, and elders of the Jews had gathered together. All of them vehemently desired to deliver Christ to death and to shed His innocent blood. When they saw Him, they exulted no differently than a lion with captured prey that it is ready to devour. And this is the second procession <note>In medieval Passion meditations, the "processions" refer to the specific journeys or forced marches Jesus made between different authorities (from the Garden to Annas, then Annas to Caiaphas, etc.).</note> of the Savior.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

LET US SEE now where the most pious mother of God has gone, and whether she will appear anywhere in public, or perhaps has deserted her son along with the Apostles. Certainly, although among the Apostles faith faltered, charity <term>charitas: the highest form of Christian love; a selfless, divine love for God and neighbor</term> grew cold, and hope wavered; though fear scattered the sheep from the shepherd and the branches were cut off from the vine, nevertheless one branch remained whole and unharmed, which is the Blessed Virgin Mary, full of the sap of faith. For it was not possible that the mother of Christ should fall into this doubt—whether Jesus were the Son of God—inasmuch as she knew herself to have conceived him without the touch of a man by the Holy Spirit. Nor could she for any reason desert him with whom she had been made one spirit in God. Indeed, the Spirit of God, with which she was full, bore witness within her concerning the Son of God, that it was necessary for him thus to suffer to enter into the glory of the Father. [...poured] out to sinners, it flowed down to the ground, and his spirit was lifted through gratitude to the Father in heaven. I beg that we turn our attention now, and with great compassion, to how miserably the Lord stood there: covered in a contemptible and ridiculous garment, likewise with a crown of thorns, a reed for a scepter, with bloody wounds, bruised limbs, and a body both horrible and filthy, trembling from the cold and dripping with blood.

...and is harder than adamant <note>original: "adamante." And so He says to the human soul:

"**Behold the man**; look upon me, so that you yourself may be looked upon by me. Love as you are loved; know me, just as I myself know you. Behold, my only-begotten son bears the fullest testimony of my love for you—the one whom I have indeed given up entirely for your sake. Neither his body, nor his soul, nor his blood was of such great value to me <note>The author suggests that God's love for humanity was so great that even the life of His Son was not "too high a price" to pay</note> that I would hesitate to hand him over for your sake. Indeed, if I could have conceived of anything more precious or anything better within my fatherly heart, I would have given that to you as well. **Behold the man**; I have given you my most high divinity within the humanity of my son, since he is one with me and in me, the same true and inseparable God, and whoever receives him, receives me. I have moreover given you my Holy Spirit, so that he might cleanse you, strengthen you, enlighten you, teach you all truth and righteousness, inflame you with his love, and likewise console you and bestow all spiritual gifts <term>charismatibus: spiritual gifts or graces granted by God for the benefit of the community</term> and virtues. For in this way I was well pleased with you, and you had found grace..."

For as we know from our daily experience, if any of us has even a slight wound or a small sore, we can hardly bear for anyone to even come near us; what then must we think of the Lord <term>JESUS Christ</term> <note>The name "Jesus" means "Savior," while "Christ" is a title meaning "The Anointed One."</note>? And because the cross was quite long, he could not carry the whole of it upon his shoulders. Thus it happened that the end of the cross, dragging against the stones with which the road was paved, created a great and horrid noise.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

In this manner, then, as was stated shortly before, the merciless Jews led Christ to Calvary <note>original: *Caluaria*, the Latin name for the site of the crucifixion, meaning "Place of the Skull"</note>, a cursed, condemned, and despicable place, filled with the stench of the corpses and bones of the dead. At the same time, we can conclude from this that the death of Christ was by far the most despised of all; and this for four reasons. 

**First**, because in that era, crucifixion was the most shameful and disgraceful kind of death, which could be inflicted only upon the most wicked of criminals. 

**Second**, because the Lord was crucified in the middle between two thieves, as if he were the leader of the thieves <note>original: *princeps latronum*</note>, so that he might be condemned by their deeds as well, and be believed to be equal in crime to those who were subjected to a similar punishment. 

**Third**, because he was killed entirely naked in the most foul place of Calvary, a treatment usually only forced upon those who were remarkably wicked. 

**Fourth**, because he was killed during the great solemnity of the Passover <note>original: *Paschæ*</note>, as if his life were so wicked and cursed that it was absolutely necessary that as

...ugh he wished to show the greatest humility, while he allowed himself to be made so naked that he did not have even a single thread remaining to cover his most honorable and modest limbs, and nothing on which to lay his holy head <note>A reference to Matthew 8:20, where Jesus says "the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." For no others condemned to death were usually driven to the cross naked, unless they were remarkably wicked and were to be put to death in a horrible manner as an example to others. 

Adam also, because of his lost innocence, hurried to cover and clothe himself with garments <note>A reference to Genesis 3, where Adam and Eve make clothes from fig leaves to hide their shame after the Fall.</note>; but Christ was stripped naked because he had preserved the purity of innocence whole and unblemished, and he had no need for any other covering.

...whatever happens to us, whether it be persecution, harassment, or contempt brought upon us by men, or the loss of loved ones, or the loss of worldly goods, or the temptation of the enemy, or internal mental anguish due to our own lack of spiritual progress: we should receive all these crosses willingly from the hands of **GOD**, stretching ourselves out upon them and saying with **St. David**: *My heart has looked for reproach and misery.* <note>Psalm 69:20 (Vulgate 68:21). original: "Improperium expectauit cor meum & miseriam." ### CHAPTER XXXVII.

Furthermore, our Lord JESUS Christ was counted among the wicked, and was hung in the middle between two thieves, as if he were the leader of thieves <note>original: "princeps latronum"</note>. This was brought about by the hostility of the Judeans <note>original: "impietas Iudaica"; in the context of this 16th-century devotional text, this refers to the historical opposition of the Jewish authorities to Christ</note>, so that CHRIST, who in himself was most innocent, might be made to appear a participant in their crimes. It was intended that he would be believed by everyone to be like those thieves in character, since he was punished with the same condemnation; thus, through the malice of others, he who was in himself most righteous might be made infamous. 

But the humble JESUS did not shrink from hanging between those for whom he desired to die. And indeed, he was numbered among the wicked on earth, so that we might be grafted into the companies <note>original: "gregibus," literally "flocks"</note> of angels in heaven. For a time, the good reputation of his name was blotted out among men, so that our names might be inscribed forever in the book of life <term>book of life; "libro vitae," a biblical concept from the Book of Revelation referring to the heavenly record of those granted eternal life</term>. He was hung between thieves, not indeed as a partner...

In this way, he showed that the power over both life and death belonged to him: and at the same time, he presented a certain preview of the future judgment, in which he would place the good on his right hand and the wicked on his left.

### CHAPTER XLII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

Now therefore, O my soul, and as many of you as have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, come now, with internal compassion and burning devotion, let us climb the blessed palm of the cross, <note>The "palm of the cross" is a poetic image representing the cross as a tree of victory and life, rather than just an instrument of death.</note> most beautifully laden with the fruit of life. ### CHAPTER XLII.

Standing also by the cross of Jesus was his most holy mother, the ever-virgin Mary. She was there not to provide any relief or tempering of his pains, but rather to cause a no small increase to them. For if any creature could have brought some comfort to the Lord hanging on the cross, none would have been as suitable for that task as his most blessed mother. But because it had been determined for Christ to succumb to a most bitter death, and to conclude his very passion <term>passione: the period of intense suffering undergone by Jesus</term> with true resignation <term>resignatione: the act of surrendering one's will entirely to God</term>—without any consolation or relief—his mother's presence provided him no comfort. Instead, it increased his sorrows, as he joined her sadness to his own pains, and from this he drew even more material for his most bitter torment <term>cruciatus: the specific physical and mental agony of crucifixion</term>. Who now, good Jesus, can understand through meditation the depth of internal grief you felt when you (who know the hearts of all) perceived all your mother's inner being <note>original: "viscera," literally 'innards' or 'bowels,' often used in the Bible to describe the seat of deep compassion or maternal love</note> and limbs...

# MEDITATIONS

<meta>catchword: heart</meta>

...measuring within himself the intolerable weight of his **passion** <term>passion: From the Latin 'passio,' meaning suffering; specifically the physical and spiritual agony of Jesus leading to his death.</term>, he spoke to the Father with a mournful voice for that reason—as if pouring out holy complaints—because he had been plunged into those horrible tortures and punishments. ...[he would] say, **"I thirst."** This word, though brief, is full of mysteries. And first, it can be taken literally. For it is naturally ordered that all those who draw their final breath feel thirst and desire drink. But what great parchedness and dryness the <term>living fountain<gloss>fons vivus</gloss></term> <note>A traditional title for Christ, referring to Him as the source of eternal life and spiritual grace.</note> experienced! He was now so exhausted and dried out by the heat of his most burning love that he said: "I am poured out like water" <note>original: "Tanquam aqua effusus sum"; Psalm 22:14.</note> and likewise, "My strength is dried up like a potsherd" <note>original: "Aruit tanquam testa virtus mea"; Psalm 22:15. A potsherd is a piece of broken ceramic, completely devoid of moisture.</note>. For he did not only pour out all his blood and release whatever moisture he had through weeping, but for our sake, he also completely consumed the very marrow of his bones and all the blood of his heart in the fire and flame of love. And so, he says with good reason that he thirsts. 

Secondly, it can also be understood spiritually, as if Christ had spoken generally to everyone, saying: **"I thirst"**—namely, for your salvation. Hence <term>Bernard<gloss>Bernardus</gloss></term> <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian monk and mystic famous for his intense, emotional writings on the suffering of Christ.</note> says: "I thirst," says Christ, "I do not grieve. O Lord, for what do you thirst? For your faith, for your joy: the concern for your souls grips me more than the torment of my body; if you will not pity me, at least pity yourselves." Scripture says: *A good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and an evil man brings forth evil from his evil treasure.* <note>original: "Bonus homo de bono thesauro cordis sui profert bonum..." A reference to Luke 6:45.</note> 

Therefore, some offer wine to Christ mixed with gall <note>original: "felle mixtum"</note>, just as the Jews did. These are the great sinners who still harbor the will to do evil. Even if they perform good works, those works are nonetheless infected with the most bitter gall; everything is corrupted and foul, taking on the taste of the tainted vessel. As soon as these works touch Christ’s palate, they are spat out by Him. Concerning these people, Moses says in the Song of Deuteronomy: *Their grape is a grape of gall, and their wine is the venom of dragons.* <note>original: "Vua eorum vua fellis, & fel draconum vinum eorum." Deuteronomy 32:32-33.</note> And St. Peter, speaking to Simon Magus <note>A figure in the New Testament who attempted to buy spiritual power with money; here used as an example of a corrupt heart.</note>, says: *I see that you are in the gall of bitterness, and your heart is not right before God.*

Others indeed reach out wine to Christ, but it is spoiled, harsh, and sour—turned into vinegar. These are the loose and frivolous people who abstain from deadly sins; however, because they take very little care regarding daily and venial <term>venialia|From 'venia' (forgiveness); these are minor sins that do not fully break one's relationship with God but weaken the soul's character.</term> sins, they abound in them and fall into them very often. This happens because they do not watch their own foundations, nor do they listen to the warnings and rebukes of the Holy Spirit; on the contrary...

For example, actions performed either out of fear, or for the sake of a reward, or out of habit, or to please other people, or for some private benefit of their own, or to obtain consolation or other gifts from God: or for other such motives, in which they seek themselves more than the pure honor of God and the fulfillment of His will. Fourth and finally, there are others who offer Jesus Christ the purest and sweetest wine. These are people who have truly died to themselves <note>original: "bene mortui"; this refers to the spiritual practice of "mortification," or dying to one's own ego and worldly desires.</note> and are fully resigned, who in all their works look only to the honor of God and seek themselves nowhere. These are the true children of God, who have forgotten their natural birth so that they may be worthy to have God as their Father. They have received the Spirit of God as a sign and proof that they are children of God, in which they also cry out, *Abba, Father* <note>original: "Abba Pater"; an Aramaic and Latin address to God emphasizing an intimate, childlike relationship, as seen in the New Testament.</note>—a cry that no one can truly utter by the testimony and judgment of the Spirit unless he is a child of God. For they have surrendered themselves entirely to God and have fundamentally resigned their will <term>resignation: the spiritual act of "resigntio," or the total surrender of one's own will and self-interest to the will of God</term>; and whatever God wishes to do with them, both in time and in eternity, is pleasing to them.

### *The curtain of the temple was torn.*

### CHAPTER LII.

FROM this point onwards, the curtain of the temple <note>original: *velum templi*. In the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem, a thick curtain separated the Holy of Holies—the most sacred space—from the rest of the building. Its tearing symbolized the opening of direct access to God through Christ's death.</note> was torn, the earth trembled, the rocks were split apart, and the sun was darkened. These wonders and portents <term>portenta: miraculous signs or omens that signal a significant divine event</term> were performed so that heaven and earth might rebuke the unbelief of the Jews, as well as all those without faith, and so that by such obvious signs they might testify that the crucified Christ was their God and Lord.

For at the terrible voice of their Creator <note>original: *conditoris*. Literally "founder" or "builder," here meaning God as the architect of the universe.</note>, all creatures trembled and groaned. It was as if they themselves wished to perish along with their Creator, feeling a weariness at serving such rebellious and ungrateful human beings any longer, and were ready to fight for their Maker <note>original: *opifice*. A craftsman or artisan; a common way of describing God's role in creating the world.</note> and avenge the wrongs done to him. As proof of this indignation, the sun changed its color, the earth shook, and even the irrational creatures—as if hungering for vengeance—were all deeply moved on account of their Creator. See here how great is the power, strength, and majesty of him who, just a moment ago, appeared so powerless and weak—

—weak and cast down. He displayed a sign in the heavens, signifying that he is the true Lord of Heaven. He also performed a sign on the earth, proclaiming and declaring that this earth is his own creation <note>original: *creaturam*. While we often think of "creatures" as animals, here it refers to the entire created world.</note>, subject and obedient to him. 

He even showed a sign in the temple, demonstrating that he is above the law, above ceremonies, and above all sacrifices. He showed that within himself resided the authority to abolish the law, just as he possessed the power to establish it. Therefore, he tore the veil <note>original: *velum*. The heavy curtain in the Temple that separated the common areas from the divine presence.</note>, so that the naked truth might be laid open—that truth which had remained hidden under the veil and coverings of the "letter" <note>original: *literae*. Referring to the "letter of the law" or the literal, outward rituals of the Old Testament as opposed to their spiritual meaning.</note>. 

At the same time, he declared through this very act that all mysteries, figures <term>figuras: symbolic "types" or people/events in the Old Testament that prefigured Christ</term>, and prophecies were now fulfilled and revealed. This occurred when he, the eternal Truth itself—for whose sake all things were written—made himself manifest to the entire world upon the cross. 

Indeed, by the tearing of the veil, he uncovered the Holy of Holies <term>sancta sanctorum: the innermost and most sacred part of the Temple, representing the immediate presence of God</term>, showing that the entire system of sacrifice, which was celebrated with the blood of cattle, was now antiquated and abolished, and no longer possessed any holiness. For Christ, the high priest, entered into the now-revealed sanctuary through his own blood. He openly offered himself upon the altar of the cross outside the town for all the people, becoming a kind of universal and perpetual sacrifice to his Father on behalf of all people who seek him.

For there are three conditions, or effects, or works of perfect love. The first work is that which forcefully snatches the lover outside of themselves. For love is strong as death <note>original: *fortis est, ut mors, dilectio*; a quotation from the Song of Solomon 8:6, emphasizing that love, like death, is an irresistible force.</note>: and just as death violently tears the soul from the body, so perfect love draws a person entirely away from themselves, so much so that they completely fail within themselves. 

The second work of love is that which attracts, or draws inward. For as it first draws the lover out of themselves, so secondly it joins and unites them to the beloved, and draws them to the beloved or into the beloved; just as the Lord says to the loving soul: "I have loved you with an everlasting love, therefore I have drawn you, taking pity on you." <note>original: *Perpetua charitate dilexi te, ideo attraxi te miserans*; a reference to Jeremiah 31:3.</note> And love <term>charity <gloss>original: charitas; in this context, it refers to the highest form of Christian love (agape), which is selfless and divine.</gloss></term> does this so truly that the lover is not where they stand or walk, but where they love. But then the pious mother replied with a lamentable voice: “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you my friends! Let me enjoy him at least in death, whom I could not keep alive. Let me, I beseech you, bestow upon his lifeless body the love and kindness that was not permitted at all during his passion. Let me now water with my tears the one to whom, in his most bitter thirst, I was not even allowed to offer a drop of water.”

"Let me satisfy <note>original: *Exatiem*, likely a transcription error for *Expleam* (let me satisfy/fill)</note> my soul in the meantime with weeping and groaning, for I could not be refreshed by his sweetest presence. And so, no small distress held them. For they did not wish to overwhelm her, already so greatly afflicted, with new sorrows. For this reason, they granted her love a space to act for a time, and they permitted her to satisfy her most burning thirst for a little while.

After this, Saint <note>original: *S.* for *Sanctus*</note> John soothed her with sweet and prudent words, requesting that she permit her son to be buried; and she consented, though certainly not without great grief. But oh, how devotedly, how afflictedly she followed the mournful funeral rites of her son, holding his sacred head, with her eyes fixed upon his face, kissing it countless times and watering it with her tears. From where, I ask, could that most sorrowful parent have obtained all those tears which she poured out today? He who the most pious...

For that very gate is closed, opened to no one, through which alone the Prince and King of Israel passed. <note>This is a traditional theological reference to the "Closed Gate" mentioned in the Prophecy of Ezekiel, which medieval scholars viewed as a symbol of Mary’s perpetual virginity—a gate through which only God could enter the world.</note>

Furthermore, this monument was in a garden: since the pure Virgin is the **enclosed garden** <note>original: *hortus conclusus*; a central medieval metaphor for the Virgin Mary, signifying a space of perfect purity protected from the "wild" world of sin.</note> of the beloved, hedged about with the fence of discernment or prudence. Indeed, she was so bathed in light and discernment that no evil could ever creep into her garden, not even under the guise of virtue. Nor was her garden open in even the smallest part where that envious and impure serpent <note>The Devil.</note> could have cast his eyes even once; he who had nevertheless dared not only to enter but also to defile the glory of the original Paradise. 

Indeed, her garden was so fruitful and so planted with every kind of herb of virtue that no space in it was vacant where any weed <note>original: *lolium*; referring to the "tares" or cockle often mentioned in biblical parables as a symbol of vice or spiritual corruption.</note> could spring up. For to the singular glory of this nourishing Virgin, there grew within her the **flower of the field** and the **lily of the valleys**, <note>Titles for Christ drawn from the Song of Solomon.</note> that excellent and aromatic **flower of Jesse** <note>original: *flos Jesse*; a reference to the prophecy of Isaiah concerning the lineage of the Messiah.</note> in whom the Holy Spirit rested, and the most lovely **rose of Jericho**. Grant also that, being stripped of all fleeting and temporary things that oppose my salvation, I may deserve to be founded and established upon Christ the Rock <term>petra Christo: a metaphor for Christ as the firm, unchanging foundation of faith</term>, that is, in you yourself. 

O sweetest Lord **JESUS** Christ, who willed to be stretched so inhumanly upon the cross that all your bones could be numbered <note>A reference to Psalm 22:17: "I can count all my bones; people stare and gloat over me," traditionally interpreted as a prophecy of the Crucifixion.</note>, grant that I may lovingly unite all my limbs and all the powers of my body and soul to you—always focused and uplifted in your most worthy praise. May my nature be so fixed to your love that I may never depart from your commandments, but [be fastened] by the nails of your fear to your cross...
